# org.casserole

Concept file. It states what this program is.

**Depends:** [java/org/casserole/config/config.spec.md](config/config.spec.md), [java/org/roux/roux.spec.md](../roux/roux.spec.md)

## A layout ask appends one locked row, and a send that changes system lines carries a wire stanza both clients can match.

The page stays open. A later ask appends as the next row. A lock on that row locks the row. The page is not a restamp of the earlier plan, not a pre-plan, and not the next stage. The draft, the pre-plan, and the plan stay as they are. The stage stays `1` / `BUILT`. The working document stays the stage map. This page does not move that stage.

A new ask is the next row. The row records the ask and the layout that follows. A lock on that row locks the row. Code for a row waits until the same sentence, or a later one, says build. `CONCAT`, the group actions, and the execution target stay as they were already built unless a row says otherwise.

The operative reading of a finesse ask is one ask: the row is added, the full cycle runs, the ask is filed, and the code is built. The row, the pre-plan, the plan, the plan copy, and the client are that one ask.

Code named on the model-door serial stays paused. The specification is taken through, approved for a pre-plan, and a formal plan is made. Then that build. A build sentence on a model-door row does not lift this pause. The plan-copy duty still holds. The pause note does not write a pre-plan and does not write the client.

The finesse workflow is filed at `aa-sdd-finesse-workflow.md`. This page stays the operative reading. A later change to that workflow is a sentence on that specification, written in the same turn.

A finesse ask still adds the row, runs the full cycle, files it, and builds the code. A side move is a dependency the new code stands on, or a change the build adds, that the named sentence did not ask for. An asked refactor stays on the path it already has. Each side move names the move, the requirement it serves, and the sibling.

A send that adds, removes, or reorders a system line carries a wire stanza in the section 12 match. The stanza names the door, then the system lines in send order, then the line in the seat the server replaces. A canvas Run, a glass send, a group send, and a pipe send are separate doors. A shared head names the doors that share it. A landing that leaves the working set as it stands carries an empty stanza and an empty side list. The plate sentence is: no side move on this plate. A neighbor line named in the plan's what-stays is named in the match.

When the other client slice is named, it quotes the stanza. A slice sentence that contradicts the stanza holds the slice commit. A wire order sits outside the surrounding measure. A shape that cannot carry a wire order comes back before the bake. Section 9 records it after that sentence has been seen. The other client's test asserts the same first system line the stanza names. Papers for the sibling move in this filing. The sibling crate stays unwritten until that catch-up is named. A side move inside a bake already named is corrected in that bake. When a slice for that behavior is already in the tree, a later client row names that slice and says the crate move for this delta waits until it is named. A client smoke says whether the sibling working set was compared to the stanza. The smoke covers the language that was run. Locked rows stay as filed. This rule extends the operative reading. It does not add a row and it does not add a law.

The decision block is a publish specification. The operative reading of a finesse ask stays. That sentence does not add a row. The page is `docs/spec/ver.1.0/aa-sdd/PD-OUTSIDE/spine/decision-block.md`.

**Truth.** The page stays open, a lock closes the row it names, and the operative ask is one cycle that files the row and builds the code. A model-door build stays paused until that serial is approved through a pre-plan and a formal plan. A changed system-line order is a wire stanza with a door, send order, and the line the server replaces. The decision block page is the publish specification, and the operative reading of an ask stays.

**Reason.** Code waits so a row is not built before a sentence says build. `CONCAT`, the group actions, and the execution target stay put so a layout ask does not silently retarget execution. The model-door pause stays in force so one build sentence cannot start that code before the specification, the pre-plan, and the plan. Side moves are listed so a dependency, or a change the named sentence did not ask for, is named with the requirement and the sibling. Separate doors keep a canvas Run, a glass send, a group send, and a pipe send from sharing an unnamed head. An empty stanza records a landing that does not change the working set. A contradicting slice is held so the stanza wins. A shape that cannot carry a wire order is sent back before the bake, and section 9 records it only after that sentence has been seen. The sibling crate waits so this client can land while the other client is written only when that catch-up is named. A side move inside a bake already named is corrected in that bake. Locked rows stay so a later sentence does not rewrite them.

**Avoidances.** Do not treat this page as a restamp, a pre-plan, or the next stage. Do not build a row before the sentence says build. Do not let a build sentence lift the model-door pause. Do not write a pre-plan or the client inside the pause note. Do not leave a side move unnamed, and do not move an asked refactor onto a new path. Do not commit a slice that contradicts the stanza. Do not bake a shape that cannot carry a wire order. Do not write the sibling crate before the catch-up is named. Do not open a new row for the side-move rule or for the decision block. Do not rewrite a locked row.

## Add Cell

When a group exists, the merge cell's main button bar carries `Add Cell`, and that button adds a new empty member to the merge group. The older ways of adding a cell stay.

The button label is `Add Cell`. It sits on the merge cell's main button bar only. A member card does not show it. An ordinary card does not show it. The canvas footer does not show it. The second bar still holds the execution target, Group, Join, and Ungroup, and it still starts hidden. New still appends one ordinary turn at the end of the canvas. Group still turns an ordinary card into member 1 and inserts a merge under it. Join still attaches an existing ordinary card to the armed member's group and leaves that card where it sits. Ungroup still pulls one card out.

Add Cell adds a new empty member to that merge's group. The new member takes the next column, one past the highest member column. It is placed with the members, before the merge. The prompt and the reply stay empty. The new member copies the last member's execution target, Ollama think choice, Grok settings, and expanded choice. When the group has no member, the new cell stays on an empty target and starts unchecked. Focus moves to the new prompt.

Both clients paint the button. There is no new package, no new public type, no new global key, no new vault column, no new channel, and no new wire message type. Nothing moves beyond the copy and the focus, and both clients make that same copy. No system line is added, removed, or reordered. The send set stays as it is.

**Truth.** `Add Cell` appears only on the merge cell's main button bar. It inserts an empty member in the next column, one past the highest member column, with the members and before the merge. The new prompt and reply are empty. The new member copies the last member's execution target, Ollama think choice, Grok settings, and expanded choice. With no member to copy, the target is empty and the expanded choice starts unchecked. Focus moves to the new prompt. New, Group, Join, and Ungroup keep their existing behavior. Both clients do this.

**Reason.** A merge group needs an obvious way to add a cell for someone who does not know the older path. That older path stays, because it will still be useful.

**Avoidances.** Do not show `Add Cell` on a member card, an ordinary card, or the canvas footer. Do not change New, Group, Join, or Ungroup. Do not show the second bar, which still starts hidden and still holds the execution target, Group, Join, and Ungroup. Do not place the new member after the merge or in any column but the next one. Do not fill the prompt or the reply. Do not skip the copy of the last member's target, think choice, Grok settings, and expanded choice. Do not give a memberless group a target or a checked expanded choice. Do not leave focus off the new prompt. Do not add, remove, or reorder a system line. Do not add a package, a public type, a global key, a vault column, a channel, or a wire message type.

## The file import

A file import streams text of any size from disk into the VT100 session or into a cell input pane. A large file gets a polite line, and the import continues. The user owns a size overflow. A thrown error is shown in red.

The read streams from disk in chunks of 8192 bytes. It does not allocate one array of the file length. The session import places the text in the VT100 session. The prompt import places the text in the cell input pane. Neither path stops at 65536 characters or at 1 MiB.

The polite line is `This file is large. The import continues.` A session file longer than 65536 bytes says that line, then the import continues. A prompt file longer than 1 MiB says that line, then the import continues. A file at either bolt does not say the line. The line is not an error. On the prompt, the landed status keeps the line ahead of `imported into turn N`.

A thrown error is the red error. The session shows the error dialog. The prompt shows the red error slide. The Rust session paints that dialog in the red ink. This row does not add a later graceful handler.

An empty session file stays refused. A binary file stays refused. A merge cell stays refused. An output-only cell stays refused. Send file stays at 65536 characters. The paste editor stays at 65536 characters. A cell written to the terminal stays at 65536 characters. The `.aetheris` deck import stays at 1 MiB.

There is no new package, no new public type, no new global key, no new vault column, no new channel, and no new wire message type. Nothing beside these two imports moves. The send set stays as it is. Both clients stream the same two imports.

**Truth.** Session import and prompt import stream from disk in 8192-byte chunks and do not stop at 65536 characters or at 1 MiB. A session file longer than 65536 bytes, and a prompt file longer than 1 MiB, show `This file is large. The import continues.` and then continue. A file exactly at either bolt does not show the line. On the prompt, that line stays ahead of `imported into turn N`. A thrown error is a red error dialog on the session and a red error slide on the prompt. An empty session file, a binary file, a merge cell, and an output-only cell stay refused. Send file, the paste editor, and a cell written to the terminal stay at 65536 characters. A `.aetheris` deck import stays at 1 MiB.

**Reason.** File import was stopping at a 65536 boundary, likely the length of one buffer. The text has to stream from disk at an arbitrary size, into the VT100 session or into a cell input pane. A large file deserves a polite warning, and the user remains responsible if a size overflow still occurs. A thrown error is simply shown in red.

**Avoidances.** Do not allocate one array of the file length. Do not stop either import at 65536 characters or at 1 MiB. Do not treat the polite line as an error. Do not say the line for a file that is exactly 65536 bytes on the session path or exactly 1 MiB on the prompt path. Do not put the polite line after `imported into turn N`. Do not add a later graceful overflow handler. Do not accept an empty session file, a binary file, a merge cell, or an output-only cell. Do not raise the 65536 limit on Send file, the paste editor, or a cell written to the terminal. Do not raise the 1 MiB limit on a `.aetheris` deck import. Do not add a package, a public type, a global key, a vault column, a channel, or a wire message type.

## The row height on a group

An added cell, and every cell in a group, follows the row-height control on the first button bar. When that count changes, the merge cell resizes to the same number of visible input rows.

That control is the saved visible-row count. The height is that count times the mono line. The line is floored at 16. Eight pixels sit under the lines. A missing count is 4. A count under 1 is 1. That is the font-height sizing function.

An added cell uses that height for its prompt. Its reply uses that height when Expanded View is unchecked. When Expanded View is checked and the reply has text, the reply stays whole, and a group cell's reply is never shorter than that height. An empty added cell therefore shows the same row window as the initial member. Add Cell still copies the last member's execution target, Ollama think choice, Grok settings, and expanded choice.

Every open cell in a group uses that function. A sequential card outside a group keeps the rule it already has. A folded card stays a brief line.

The merge cell has no prompt. Its reply pane uses that same height, including when the reply is empty. When Expanded View is checked and the reply has text, the reply stays whole, and the pane is never shorter than that height. Changing the row control changes that height, so the merge resizes with the new count.

There is no new package, no new public type, no new global key, no new vault column, no new channel, and no new wire message type. Nothing beside this height moves. The send set stays as it is. Both clients use the same function. `Add Cell` stays on the merge bar.

**Truth.** The visible-row count, missing as 4 and never under 1, times a mono line floored at 16, plus 8 pixels under the lines, is the height. An added cell's prompt uses it. An unchecked reply uses it. A checked reply that has text stays whole and is never shorter than it. Every open group cell uses it. The merge has no prompt, and its reply uses that height even when empty, with the same floor when Expanded View is checked and the reply has text. A sequential card outside a group is unchanged. A folded card stays a brief line. Both clients do this.

**Reason.** An added cell was not taking the same height as the initial cell. Every cell in a group, including the merge when the count changes, has to follow the visible-row control.

**Avoidances.** Do not size an added cell differently from the initial member. Do not let a group reply fall shorter than the row window when Expanded View is checked and the reply has text. Do not clip a checked reply that has text. Do not give the merge a prompt. Do not leave an empty merge reply off that window. Do not apply this function to a sequential card outside a group. Do not grow a folded card past a brief line. Do not drop the Add Cell copy of the last member's execution target, Ollama think choice, Grok settings, and expanded choice. Do not use a line under 16 pixels or a pad other than 8. Do not treat a missing count as anything but 4, or a count under 1 as anything but 1. Do not add a package, a public type, a global key, a vault column, a channel, or a wire message type.

## The button word

A button word turns emerald while the pointer is on that button, and the word returns to the color that button already had when the pointer leaves. The tooltip waits 50 ms longer.

A button word turns `#00FF66` while the pointer is on that button. The leave restores the color that button already had. The shift is immediate. The tooltip wait grows by 50 ms. The Java client goes from 750 ms to 800 ms. The Rust client goes from 0.50 s to 0.55 s. The word does not wait on that timer.

The plate fill stays. The plate stroke stays. P and C rest white. Yes rests black. No rests white. A selectable tab keeps its word. A menu title keeps its word. The Connected chip stays. An arrow mark has no word. File, Tools, and Help stay.

There is no new package and no new public type. The Java hover is seated in private. The Rust side keeps the word color and the hover seat in private. There is no new global key, no new vault column, no new channel, no new wire message type, no new color key, no new library, and no settings-file edit. The experimental toolkit feature is the button theme seat. Nothing beside this word and this wait moves. The send set stays as it is. The Java client moves first. The Rust client moves second.

**Truth.** On hover, a button word becomes `#00FF66` immediately, and on leave it returns to the color that button already had. The tooltip wait grows by 50 ms: 750 ms becomes 800 ms on the Java client, and 0.50 s becomes 0.55 s on the Rust client. The word does not wait on that timer. Plate fill and plate stroke stay. P and C rest white. Yes rests black. No rests white. A selectable tab keeps its word. A menu title keeps its word. The Connected chip stays. An arrow mark has no word. File, Tools, and Help stay. Both clients carry this.

**Reason.** A button under the pointer has to show an emerald word, and the tooltip has to wait a little longer so the word can be read. The word itself must not wait on that timer.

**Avoidances.** Do not delay the color shift. Do not change the tooltip wait by any amount but 50 ms. Do not make the word wait on the tooltip timer. Do not change the resting colors: P and C white, Yes black, No white. Do not recolor a selectable tab, a menu title, the Connected chip, or an arrow mark. Do not change File, Tools, or Help. Do not change the plate fill or the plate stroke. Do not add a color key, a library, a package, a public type, a global key, a vault column, a channel, or a wire message type. Do not edit a settings file.

## The tab rule

A divider sits between Connect and the SSH tab. The two tab buttons stand apart.

The open bar carries the line. The folded row stays as it is. The folded rule stays on the menu, after Aetheris and before File, Tools, and Help.

The Java client seats a one-pixel panel on the south of the open head. The ink is the panel foreground. The Java default of that ink is `#dcdcdc`. The live theme may already hold another panel foreground. This plate reads no home file and adds no color key. The line leaves with the open bar.

The Rust client calls `separator()` after the door note and before the SSH tab. The parent column is vertical, so the line is horizontal. That is the same call the folded menu divider uses.

The menu stays. The words stay SSH and Aetheris. The Aetheris tab stays disabled until the mux answers. Connect stays the first button of the open row. The grip stays. The thinking text stays clear. The emerald word stays. The tooltip wait stays.

There is no new package, no new public type, and no new public method. The Java line is a private field. There is no new global key, no new vault column, no new channel, no new wire message type, no new color key, no new library, no settings-file edit, and no dependency-manifest edit. Nothing beside this line moves. The send set stays as it is. Both clients carry this.

**Truth.** On the open bar, a divider sits between Connect and the SSH tab, and the two tab buttons stand apart. The folded row is unchanged, and its rule stays after Aetheris and before File, Tools, and Help. Java draws a one-pixel panel on the south of the open head in the panel foreground, whose default is `#dcdcdc`, and reads no home file. The line leaves with the open bar. Rust draws a horizontal `separator()` after the door note and before the SSH tab, the same call the folded menu divider uses. Connect stays the first button of the open row. The Aetheris tab stays disabled until the mux answers. The words stay SSH and Aetheris.

**Reason.** Connect and the SSH tab were sitting against each other. A divider has to separate them, and the two tab buttons have to stand apart, on both clients.

**Avoidances.** Do not put the new line on the folded row. Do not move the folded rule from its place after Aetheris and before File, Tools, and Help. Do not paint the Java line thicker than one pixel, or in any ink but the panel foreground. Do not add a color key or read a home file for the ink. Do not leave the line up after the open bar folds away. Do not make the Rust line vertical. Do not use a different separator than the folded menu divider. Do not move Connect off the first place on the open row. Do not enable the Aetheris tab before the mux answers. Do not change the grip, the clear thinking text, the emerald word, or the tooltip wait. ## The bar press

A press on a pulled-out scroll bar leaves the wheel on the master canvas.

A touch does this, and a drag does this. The Swing client returns focus to the canvas scroller. The Rust client leaves the wheel on the canvas. A press on the text still focuses that text. The bar still drags. The hit strip is the scroll bar width, on the right. These panes scroll vertically.

The Swing helper is `barHit`. The Rust helper is `bar_press`. Both clients change.

**Truth.** Pressing or dragging the overlay scroll bar does not take the wheel off the master canvas. Pressing the text still focuses the text. The bar still drags. The strip is the bar width, on the right, and the panes scroll vertically.

**Reason.** A press meant to grab the bar was moving focus onto the bar, so the next wheel notch scrolled the wrong pane.

**Avoidances.** Do not steal focus from a text press. Do not disable the drag. Do not move the strip off the right edge or off the scroll-bar width. Do not make these panes scroll horizontally. Do not add a package, a public type, a public method, a shortcut, a stored column, a channel, a wire type, a color key, or a library. Do not edit the application yaml or the Rust manifest.

## The locked sapphire

The thinking body stays the lighter sapphire in both clients. A later change does not retint a locked color or resize a locked control unless that change names the element.

Swing already wears bytes 115, 174, and 255 on both strips. Rust `THINK_BODY` paints those bytes. The yellow body name is gone. Card replies stay yellow. Button sizes stay. The menus stay.

The Rust client changes. The Swing client already has the color and stays.

**Truth.** The thinking body is rgb(115, 174, 255) on the notebook strip and on the VT100 strip, in both clients. Card replies stay yellow. A later change may retint a color or resize a control only when it names that element.

## The seat

EditMemory is the container. It wraps UndoManager. The limit is 100. An edit stores the text and the cursor before the change, and the text and the cursor after it. note pushes when the text differs. The same text only moves the cursor. undo and redo swap that stored text. The caller writes text and cursor into the widget that is live. applying stops the listener from pushing the write it just applied. sync remembers a rebuilt widget without pushing. discard drops the stack.

A canvas cell id maps to one EditMemory. The map is RAM. A deleted cell drops its seat. Clear turns drops the seats of the cells that left. The prompt binds Ctrl-Z and Shift-Ctrl-Z while it is focused. The initial text is synced, not recorded. Import through setText is one step.

ChatShell keeps a draft seat and a visit seat. A history hop discards the visit stack and syncs the canonical line. The draft stack stays parked with the draft. The first text change that leaves history mode adopts the visit seat as the draft seat. Enter and bare Escape drop both stacks. Ctrl-Z is byte 0x1A. Redo is ESC [ 1 ; 6 Z. ## Proof

A quiet compile that does not run tests passes. The window is not opened. The live call is not made. A pool turn is not sent.

**Truth.** Clear and add stay inside the region lock, the provider call runs after the release, and the View bar marks every match in that reply without searching the canvas.

**Reason.** A concat join that holds the Roux region across both the pool prompt and the Ollama complete cannot overlap those two calls, and a large reply needs a find that walks the text already in the window.

**Avoidances.** No third mux channel, no new pool reason, no parallel pipe chain, no canvas search from the View bar, no lower-cased copy of the reply, and no more than 2000 stored matches.

A pool session keeps the column. A later Run sends the tail.

**semantic-key:** PK-7803

## Goal

Stop paying Heavy for two copies of the same column. The first prompt of a pool session carries the working set. A later prompt on that session carries the tail. A full paste remains the path when the column no longer extends the hold. Good enough is the goal. The accepted full pastes are listed below.

**semantic-key:** PK-4957

## Out of this build

`session/load` stays uncalled. Deleting abandoned session folders stays out. A persisted-session use case stays out. A thinner wire execute stays out. The frame still carries the full working set, and `AmwpCodec.fits` stays the frame check. Roux is unchanged. The region still receives the full list on the short lock. The walker, the five pool reasons, the child gate, the semaphore of 3, the idle reap, `num-ctx`, air-gap, and the Grok URL stay as they are. A third mux channel, a new lamina lane, a new package, a public type, a vault column, and a G-key stay out. The window is not opened. A live call is not sent. A pool turn is not sent.

**semantic-key:** PK-4958

## The edit

`AetherisNotebookPanel` mints one `poolBootId` at construction, a random UUID. The panel is built with the desktop, so a new app start mints a new id and an SSH reconnect on the same window keeps the id. `assemble` writes it on `ExecuteBody.poolBoot` when the provider is `pool`. Other providers leave the field empty.

`AmwpToon` gives `ExecuteBody` a `poolBoot` field. Encode writes `pool_boot:` when the field is non-empty. Decode reads it. Absent means empty. An empty boot on the server keeps a new session on every prompt, which is the earlier behavior.

`PoolChat.prompt` gains the boot string between the text and the think flag. One implementor.

`AmwpFacade.runPool` passes `req.poolBoot` and the same `poolPromptText` string it already builds. The slice happens inside the binding. The façade still hands the whole string across.

`PoolChatServer` gives the child `heldBoot`, `flatHeld`, and `holdValid`. They live on that SSH user's child, beside `sessionId`. The prompt gate still wraps the whole prompt, so two pool cells for one user stay in order and the hold updates on that same stack.

A hold extends when all of these are true: `holdValid` is set, the boot string is non-empty and equals `heldBoot`, the process is alive and initialized, `sessionId` is non-empty, `flatHeld` is non-empty, and the new working-set string starts with `flatHeld` and is longer than `flatHeld`. The child then skips `session/new` and sends `session/prompt` with the substring after `flatHeld`.

Every other prompt drops the hold, calls `session/new`, and sends the whole string. Dropping the hold clears `holdValid`, `flatHeld`, `heldBoot`, and `sessionId`. The process stays up. `initialize` still runs once on that process.

On a clean success the binding stores the boot, sets `holdValid` when the boot is non-empty, and sets `flatHeld` to the whole working-set string plus one assistant block when the stored reply is non-empty. The block is the same three-part shape `poolPromptText` uses for an assistant turn: the word `assistant`, a newline, the reply text, a newline, and a blank line. An empty reply adds no block. The reply is the concatenated message chunks. Thought text stays out of it.

A cancel, a stop, a failure, a `too-large` from the binding, or an exception drops the hold and does not align. The cell still ends on the path it already uses. The five reasons stay. No prompt text is logged.

A death before any forwarded chunk still retries once. Respawn drops the hold. The retry initializes, opens a new session, and sends the whole working set, including when the dead attempt had been a tail. A death after a forwarded chunk, a second death, a parse, a payload, a tool refusal, and an auth failure still do not retry, and they drop the hold. The fifteen-minute reap still destroys the process. The next prompt is a new child, a new session, and the whole working set, on the same desktop boot.

`session/load` is not called. Old session folders under `~/.grok/sessions` for the pool directory stay where Grok wrote them.

The pool plan package 3 keeps the sentence that a reused session would keep the previous prompt. The later sentence says this cut reuses the id only for a tail, and opens a new id when the hold does not extend.

**semantic-key:** PK-4959

## Accepted full pastes

These cut a new session and send the working set. They are the goal on those runs.

The desktop boot id changed, or the boot field is empty. The child was just spawned, reaped, or respawned. The previous prompt failed, was cancelled, or died. The next working set does not start with the held text. That is a re-run of the same card, because that card's own reply stays off its send while the hold already ends with the reply. It is also an edit, an exclude, a state change, a mood change, or a pipe change above the tail. It is a card higher in the column. It is another canvas on the same user, because one child holds one transcript. It is a same-group sibling, because the walker leaves siblings out, so the second member does not start where the first ended. It is a later card whose new context includes a merge this session never saw. The next working set equals the hold and the tail would be empty.

A jump downward across several unrun cards is a tail when the shared prefix still matches. The tail can be several role blocks. It is one text block on `session/prompt`, the same role-line shape as the first paste.

**semantic-key:** PK-4960

## Gotchas the code keeps

The frame can still fail `AmwpCodec.fits` on the full working set. The tail does not shrink that frame.

Tool refusals stay inside a held session for the life of that id. A new id drops them from the next prompt. This build does not strip them.

The prefix is reconstructed on the server from the text it sent and the reply it stored. It is not read back from the session folder. A pipe token inside a stored reply that resolves to different text on the next Run breaks the prefix, and that Run pastes the working set.

Grok's own system prompt and tool list still ride inside the session on every model call. The saving is the duplicate column, not a smaller agent prompt.

Two pool members of one group stay serial on the child gate. The second member's working set fails the prefix, so it opens its own session. The first member's session is left on disk.

**semantic-key:** PK-4961

## Proof

A quiet compile that does not run tests passes. The window is not opened. The live call is not made. A pool turn is not sent.

**Truth.** One desktop boot id keeps a pool session only while the next working set is a longer string that starts with the held text, and every other prompt opens a new session and sends the whole working set.

**Reason.** Pasting the same column twice makes Heavy pay for two copies, and a tail is the saving only when the hold still matches.

**Avoidances.** No `session/load`, no thinner wire frame, no Roux change, no new pool reason, no stripped tool refusals, and no prompt text in the log.

**semantic-key:** PK-7932

Delete on the footer removes a normal card. An armed card in a group removes that whole group and the merge.

**semantic-key:** PK-7804

## Goal

The existing footer Delete button reads the armed card. A normal card leaves as one row. A card that belongs to a group takes every cell of that group, including the merge.

**semantic-key:** PK-4962

## What stays

Group, Join, Ungroup, Duplicate group, and Shift-Ctrl-G stay. The sapphire paint stays the rule already filed: the whole run lights when the merge is armed, and one card lights when a member is armed. Clear turns stays the wipe that leaves one empty cell. The copy icon stays. The pool session hold stays on the server. Pipe token text stays as written. Parent pointers stay as stored. Another canvas stays. A replica stays. The copy methods from the clipboard work stay. There is no confirm dialog. There is no new button.

**semantic-key:** PK-4963

## The landing

The product files are `VaultStore` and `AetherisNotebookPanel`.

`deleteTurns(canvasId, cellIds, remaining)` performs the earlier one-cell writes for many ids in one transaction: trace rows for each id, the cell row on this canvas, turn indexes from 1 on the cells that remain, and the canvas order. `deleteTurn` delegates to that method with a one-element list. Parent pointers and prompt text stay as stored.

On the panel, the removal set is computed from the armed card on the canvas that is showing.

An empty group id puts that one cell in the set. A set group id puts every cell on this canvas with that group id into the set, members and the merge. Column position does not split the set. The button is enabled when the set is non-empty and smaller than the canvas. A canvas of one cell stays disabled. A group that is the entire canvas stays disabled. The listener still calls `deleteFocusedTurn`. That method recomputes the set and returns when the button would be off.

Before the worker runs, on the Swing thread, the ids are buried. `persistAll`, `persistQuiet`, and `saveCells` skip a buried id, because `saveCell` inserts when the update matches zero rows. `applyPendingNow` drops a buried id out of the held answers and does not paint it. A RUNNING cell in the set is marked STOPPED and sent the same `TYPE_CANCEL` frame Stop already sends, when that user's connector is open. The spinner stops when that user has no RUNNING cell left. Held answers for those ids are removed. `chainQueue` is cleared when it contains any removed id. The group timer for that group id is stopped and removed. `armedGroupSource` is cleared when it names a removed id.

The worker calls `deleteTurns`. On success the Swing thread drops the cells from the canvas and from the order, moves `focusedCellId` to the survivor at the first removed index, or to the last survivor when the set sat at the end, forgets the Grok entries, drops the thinking holders, rebuilds, and refreshes the inspector. The burial stays. The status line says `deleted turn on` plus the canvas name for a normal card, and `deleted group on` plus the canvas name for a group.

On failure the burial for those ids is lifted, the button is refreshed, and the status line says `delete turn failed` or `delete group failed` with the SQL message.

The Delete tip, through `buttonTip`, says a normal card removes that one row, a card in a group removes that whole group and its merge, the survivors are numbered from 1, the button stays off when the canvas would be left empty, and pipe tokens stay as written. The sentence that said the merge sink stays is replaced by this tip.

**semantic-key:** PK-4964

## Accepted catch

A folded pool stream on a card that is about to leave can still hold chunks in the assistant area. The row is deleted. The chunks are not copied anywhere by this click. A late frame for a buried id is dropped. The server still drops a reply after the cancel by `stillMine`.

A pipe token on a survivor keeps its digits. The index then resolves against the cells that remain. That shift is the earlier renumber rule, kept.

Deleting the group that sat inside a pool hold does not send a session message. The next working set that no longer extends the hold starts a session by the tail rule already landed.

**semantic-key:** PK-4965

## Gotchas the code keeps

The burial list lives for the session. A failed delete removes only the ids of that attempt.

A group delete and a one-cell delete share `deleteTurns`. The order of ids in the list does not change the survivor order. The survivor list is the canvas order with those ids removed.

The merge is included because its group id matches. A cell on another canvas is outside the scan.

An unreadable member, a ghost, and every I E P O state ride with the set. State does not split the delete.

**Truth.** Footer Delete removes one ungrouped row, or every cell on this canvas that shares the armed card's group id, in one vault transaction, and it refuses a delete that would leave the canvas empty.

**Reason.** The armed card is the operator's selection, so either arm of a group has to take the members and the merge together, and a late save must not insert a row the delete just removed.

**Avoidances.** No confirm dialog, no new button, no replacement cell, no session message from the delete, and no delete that reaches another canvas.

**semantic-key:** PK-4966

`shell_model:` replies with `shell_model_result:`, then a `model:` line and a `think:` line.

`shell_model_set:` reads a `model:` line and a `think:` line. It calls `applyConsoleModel`, writes `model <id>\r\n` on the VT100, and replies with the same result body. A missing line is empty. The reply does not include the base URL.

**semantic-key:** PK-4973

**semantic-key:** PK-4974

`completeTurn` returns the assistant text. It runs the cell refusal, opens the bantha region, places the host system line, holds Roux and releases that lock, then routes. # Program map

This page is the map the three programs share. Casserole, Aetheris Shell, and aetheris-client are one product and one wire. A builder reads this page first, then the piece page that owns a procedure. The piece page does not get to invent a second contract. This page does not get to leave a shared rule, a number, a default, a refusal, or a reason behind on the grounds that a piece page will mention it later.

The prose here is a retranslation of the product constitution, the technical specification, the notebook working specification, and the first-build plan and pre-plan. Where those writings disagree, both sentences are stated, and the sentence the present source uses is named when a source names it. History is folded into the reason. A private name, a password, a real key, a private model name, and a shop ritual stay off the page. The published ports, the published model, and the published endpoints below are the configuration a stranger is allowed to see.

A from-scratch build of a silo is the part page named at the end of this map. This page is the shared contract that build is not allowed to drift from.

---

**semantic-key:** PK-5407

## The product is a sovereign desktop for thought, code, and cognitive history, and it was built as a terminal host first.

Aetheris is a sovereign desktop for thought, code, and cognitive history. Those belong to the operator. A cloud model is a target the operator may call. It is not the landlord of the history. The same sentence, said at greater length, is the declaration: thoughts, code, and cognitive history are not rented from a vendor's web chat. The shift is from a passive stream to an active desktop. Intelligence is fast because the work sits on the desktop. Context is controlled because the operator chooses the working set. Memory endures because the history can sit on the operator's machine.

The phrase that calls the vault zero-knowledge means only that. The history sits on the operator's hardware. Vendors do not hold the canvas. A burner is not retained. The phrase is not a cryptographic proof system, and it is not a proof protocol. "Local vault" in the product constitution is the same refusal under a shorter name.

Three pillars stand on one pipe. The agentic pillar is a local host. Tools live on that host. The operator can see them, bound them, and keep the traces. The canvas pillar is a notebook of cells. The operator chooses what enters the next prompt. Memory endures when the operator chooses the durable vault. The terminal pillar is a real VT100 session on the same login. It stays a terminal. The speed is the desktop. The control is the working set. The endurance is the local vault.

The build order is the order of those pillars, not a stack of optional themes. First the terminal host: a login, a paged memory for that login, a local model call, logging, thread lanes, and a desktop window that was only a terminal. Then a sovereign notebook on that same login, with its own client vault and a framed scope beside the terminal bytes. Then groups, pipes, and a second model door on the host's one provider interface. Then a second client, written in another language, that speaks the same wire and keeps its own vault file. The notebook and the VT100 session both have to keep working on a login that speaks the framed protocol. A login that does not speak it stays a raw terminal.

The failures the desktop is built to close are these. Disposable history is closed by a client vault the operator owns, including search, branching, export, and a cold start that does not need the vendor. An all-or-nothing choice between a local engine and a cloud engine is closed by a per-cell target and by a burner pin; a burner is not safe to send to a cloud model by default. A black-box context that drags every old turn into the next prompt is closed by four inclusion states, by a ghost treatment of the excluded state, and by a working-set preview. There is no scope tag on a cell. Parallel models and merged results are a later group, not the first notebook. Cloud agents the operator cannot see are closed by keeping tools on the local host and traces in the operator's vault. Flows that cannot be debugged on the box are closed by letting the canvas author the work and letting the terminal remain the ops view.

The ordinary uses are the same shape. An offline-first local engine with local tools. A hybrid canvas that can target the local engine and, when the second door is actually in use, a remote model, without moving the history. The terminal host exists before the notebook, the notebook exists before groups and pipes and the second model door, and the second client speaks the wire the host already defined. Do not collapse the terminal into the notebook, or the notebook into the terminal. Do not describe groups, pipes, the tool channel, or the branch channels as the path a cell runs today. ## Three programs share the product, and each one refuses the other's job.

Where a language cannot carry a rule, the specification records the alternative, and the contract stays the one set. The recorded alternative that already exists is the vault status rewrite described with the vaults: one client rewrites a stored running status on load, and the other does not.

Casserole is the Java server. It is the SSH host, the terminal chat, the paged memory, the model router, and the agent host. It stays a correct agent host when no client is connected. It does not open a client vault. It does not start either client. It does not grow a client window. The terminal chat still runs when the canvas scope is absent. The server writes terminal bytes on the terminal channel and canvas bytes on the canvas channels. The server façade that writes those canvas bytes is not the vault.

Aetheris Shell is the Java client. The window name is Aetheris Shell. The class is `SshClientApp`. It holds the Java vault and the Swing canvas. It does not start the server. It does not boot the server process. It does not grow its own model stack. Conversation traffic goes to the host over the wire. All model conversation from this client hits the host's model path. Adapters for a cell identifier, a cancel, and a working set are allowed. A second model stack is not. The shell does not open the Rust vault file.

aetheris-client is the Rust client. It is a program a person runs. The window is egui on winit. It speaks the same wire. Its vault is its own file. It does not open the Java vault file, including the H2 file named `vault.mv.db`. It does not start the server. It does not grow a second model stack. Its terminal grid is this client's grid. The SSH library stays behind the host side of the terminal core, so the grid the operator sees is not a second copy of the server's session object.

The three silos named for a published specification are `casserole-server`, `aetheris/java`, and `aetheris/rust`. A published specification of each silo carries the detail of that silo. A from-scratch build from those pages matches the program. Disk size is not a reason to leave a detail out. This map is the shared prose. It is not a second copy of every procedure.

What each program refuses, said so it cannot be softened later:

- The server does not open a client vault, Java or Rust.
- The Java client does not start the server, and the Rust client does not start the server.
- The Rust client does not open the Java H2 file.
- Neither client grows a second model stack.
- Neither client writes canvas frames into the terminal byte stream.
- The server does not pretend the terminal pack is canvas history.
- The server does not add a second disk writer to a user's terminal memory.
- A client does not route cells by a scope tag.
- A raw terminal login still reaches the terminal.

**Truth.** One server, two clients, one wire, one host reference. The server is the agent host even with nobody connected. Each program refuses the job that belongs to another: vaults stay in the clients, the process start of the server stays out of the clients, and the model path stays on the host.

**Reason.** If the server opened the vault, the host would stop being correct when the vault was absent, and two languages would fight over one file. If a client grew a model stack, the same prompt would mean two different calls. If the Rust client opened the Java file, the two vault writers would no longer be two stores. The wire is the only shared mutable surface, and it is a contract, not a file.

**Avoidances.** Do not start the server from a client script. Do not point the Rust vault at `vault.mv.db`. Do not add a client-side model router that calls the engine directly. Do not let a surface difference become a frame difference. Do not treat a missing client as a broken host.

## The wire is a little-endian framed protocol on one SSH login, and a payload over 1 MiB is refused.

The wire is AMWP. One SSH login carries two scopes. Scope T is the terminal. Scope A is the canvas and the agent calls. Terminal bytes stay opaque. A canvas frame is not placed inside the terminal stream. A login that does not speak the protocol stays a raw terminal. The canvas scope stays unavailable on that login. A raw SSH client still reaches the terminal. There is no WebSocket beside this login.

The demux sits in bytes, in front of the terminal connector. The mux stream is not decoded as text. The terminal widget sees only the concatenated payloads of the terminal channel. The widget is not subclassed to parse frames, and it is not reparented out of the terminal split tree. On the server, the mux sits around the existing command pipes. The terminal chat writes VT100 bytes on the terminal channel. The canvas façade writes the canvas channels. The façade is not the vault. The server's listen loop and the terminal chat share the terminal input lane. The framed protocol does not become a new thread of its own.

The client may send Init. If there is no valid reply carrying the magic, the session is a raw terminal. The terminal widget is never wrapped in that case. An OpenSSH login to the host port stays the raw terminal it was before the notebook existed. The documented shape is `ssh -p 2222 user@localhost`.

The frame is little-endian. The header is sixteen bytes, then the payload.

The magic is one byte at offset 0, value `0xAE`. The version is one byte at offset 1, value `1`. The channel identifier is two bytes at offset 2. The type is one byte at offset 4. The flags are one byte at offset 5. Two reserved bytes sit at offset 6. The payload length is four bytes at offset 8 and counts the payload only. The CRC32C is four bytes at offset 12. The payload begins at offset 16.

The CRC32C covers the first twelve header bytes, which are the half-open range from offset 0 up to but not including the CRC field, plus the payload. The CRC field itself is not part of that twelve-byte prefix. A change that adds, removes, or reorders a system line on this wire updates the product constitution, the specification, and every implementation of that line in the same change.

The types that are locked are these. Init is `0x00`. Data is `0x01`. Prune is `0x02`. End of stream is `0x03`. Error is `0x04`. Cancel is `0x05`. Delta is `0x06`. Keepalive is `0x09`. Delta is one thinking chunk or one content chunk. The writings do not assign `0x07` or `0x08`. The earlier technical specification's type list omits Delta and jumps from Cancel to Keepalive. The product constitution includes Delta. The present wire is the constitution's list.

The flags that are defined are these. Bit 0 means ephemeral. Bit 1 means a compressed payload, and that compression is deferred. The technical specification names the deferred compression as zstd. The constitution names the bit as compressed payload deferred and does not name the algorithm. Bit 2 means more fragments. Present writers send flags `0`. The fragment flag is defined. Present writers do not split a body. Present writers do not set the ephemeral bit, and they do not compress. The burner pin on a cell is a vault fact, not a flag these writers currently send.

The maximum payload is 1 MiB, which is 1,048,576 bytes. Two writings describe what happens above that cap. The technical specification says a larger message fragments, using the more-fragments bit. The product constitution says a payload over 1 MiB is refused, and present writers do not split a body. The constitution is the sentence that follows the source. The present rule is refusal. The fragment bit stays defined so the later possibility is not deleted from the header. A builder does not implement fragmentation in the present writers, and a builder does not accept an oversized payload.

Every Scope A payload begins with a fragment index, a fragment count, and a sixteen-byte cell identifier, then the body. The technical specification fixes the widths: the fragment index is an unsigned thirty-two-bit integer, the fragment count is an unsigned thirty-two-bit integer, and the cell identifier is a UUID in sixteen raw bytes, not a text form. The prefix is inside the payload, so it counts toward the 1 MiB cap. A present writer that does not split still sends the prefix. One fragment is a count of one, not an excuse to omit the fields.

The channels are these.

Channel `0x0001` is Scope T. Its payload is opaque terminal octets. The terminal widget concatenates those payloads and sees nothing else.

Channel `0x0002` is Scope A. It is the control channel: create, read, update, delete, state, execute, cancel, and traces.

Channel `0x0003` is Scope A. It is the model stream for a cell.

Channel `0x0004` is Scope A. It is the tool channel. It is locked direction. It is not the present execute path.

Channels `0x0100` and above are Scope A. They are parallel branch streams. They are locked direction. They are not the present execute path. When that path exists, the server allocates the next free channel at or above `0x0100` in the Init acknowledgement. The client does not hardcode those numbers. Channels from `0x0005` through `0x00FF` are not assigned by these writings.

One execute is in flight for a cell. The backpressure rule is that one in-flight execute per cell identifier. The notebook cut does not invent a second acknowledgement protocol. Cancel names that cell. The cancel payload carries the cell identifier. The host aborts the lane work for that cell. The abort is best-effort, `cancel(true)` on the lane handle, the same family of cancel as the terminal's own interrupt. The terminal's own interrupt stays on the terminal. A Ctrl+C in the terminal pane cancels that pane's terminal chat. It is not the canvas cancel, and the canvas cancel is not that keystroke.

Keepalive does not write memory and does not change the terminal mode. The technical specification adds the interval and the lock it must not touch: a keepalive goes out after two seconds of idle, and it does not take the terminal pack's exclusive lock and does not change the terminal chat's mode. The constitution does not restate the two seconds. The interval stands from the technical specification. The memory rule stands from both: keepalive is not a write.

The execute body is the working set the client assembled, the cell identifier, the execution target, the knobs, and whether tools are enabled. The knobs are temperature, maximum tokens, and top-p. The technical specification names the tools flag `tool_calling_enabled`. The body is TOON inside a length-prefixed envelope. The host does not read the client vault to build that set. The host does not fetch the H2 file, and it does not fetch the Rust file. A prune frame may preview a working set before a run. The host does not persist that preview.

There is no JSON on a new canvas path, a new framed-protocol path, or a new object path unless a concrete use earns it. The envelope is length-prefixed records. The structured body is TOON. The terminal's existing JSON reply formatter is preserved. It stays on the terminal. It is not the canvas encoding.

The first notebook cut is allowed to turn one completion call into one data frame and one end frame on the stream channel. It does not require a reactive stream type in the client packages. Delta remains the locked type for one thinking chunk or one content chunk when a stream sends chunks. A builder does not pretend the first cut already split tokens if the completion was one shot, and a builder does not delete Delta from the header because that first cut allowed one shot.

**Truth.** One little-endian frame, magic `0xAE`, version `1`, a sixteen-byte header, CRC32C over the first twelve bytes plus the payload, a 1 MiB payload cap that is a refusal in the present writers, flags sent as zero, a Scope A prefix of two unsigned thirty-two-bit counts and a sixteen-byte cell identifier, and the channels above. One execute in flight. Cancel names the cell. Keepalive is not a memory write. The execute body is the client's working set, not a vault fetch.

**Reason.** Two applications on one login need a demux that cannot be confused with terminal bytes. Opaque terminal bytes keep every existing terminal client working. A hard cap that refuses, rather than a fragmenter the writers do not implement, keeps both sides honest about what they actually send. Putting the working set in the execute body means the host never has to open a client file to know what the operator chose.

**Avoidances.** Do not fragment in the present writers. Do not accept a payload over 1 MiB. Do not UTF-8-decode the mux. Do not subclass the terminal widget to find frames. Do not put a canvas frame inside the terminal stream. Do not let keepalive write the pack or change mode. Do not persist a prune preview. Do not hardcode a branch channel. Do not treat the tool channel or the branch channels as the path a cell uses now. Do not invent types `0x07` or `0x08`. Do not put JSON on a new canvas object. Do not add a second acknowledgement protocol.

## A canvas is a notebook of cells, inclusion is four states, and groups and pipes are specified without being the present execute path.

A workspace holds canvases. A canvas holds cells. A cell has an identifier, an order, a parent, a branch, a column, an execution target written `provider/model`, a context state, a burner pin, payloads, knobs, and an execution status. The identifier is a UUID. The order is the notebook order. The turn index is the display number, dense per canvas, and it is not the terminal memory's sequence number. A null parent is the root of a column. The branch defaults to `main`. The column is the interface column. A null group means a sequential cell. The group identifier is the parallel-group field, and it belongs to the later group work. The payloads are the prompt and the response, or empty when the cell is a burner. The knobs are temperature, maximum tokens, top-p, and whether tools are enabled. The status is one of idle, running, completed, failed, or interrupted.

The context states are locked, and the stored tokens are `INCLUDED`, `EXCLUDED`, `INPUT_ONLY`, and `OUTPUT_ONLY`. `INCLUDED` means later prompts receive the prompt and the response, the turn is kept for the operator unless it is a burner, and the cell is on the canvas. `EXCLUDED` means later prompts receive neither side, the turn is kept unless it is a burner, and the cell stays on the canvas dimmed. That dim is the ghost. Ghost is a modifier of `EXCLUDED`, not a fifth state. `INPUT_ONLY` means later prompts receive the prompt, the turn is kept, and the cell is on the canvas. `OUTPUT_ONLY` means later prompts receive the response, the turn is kept, and the cell is on the canvas. The status tokens are `IDLE`, `RUNNING`, `COMPLETED`, `FAILED`, and `INTERRUPTED`. There is no scope tag on a cell and no tag-based routing. The client rebuilds the working set on every execute and can show that set. The host does not invent a second copy of the operator's choice.

On the Java canvas the four states are one radio group. Exactly one is selected. The first cell button is included, and it is the default. The second is excluded. The third is input only. The fourth is output only. The pin on the cell is the burner. It is not a fifth segment. The footer runs the focused cell, or a checked batch. The footer inserts a new turn below. The footer toggles the working-set preview. The graph control is absent. It is not drawn as a disabled mystery. It appears only with the later graph work. The footer options are maximum tokens, temperature, and top-p. The burner is not a footer option. The footer spinner is the value of the selected option. The layout mock treats `100` as the default maximum tokens. A checkbox is multi-select for a batch run, an export, or a chain. It is not the four-state control. Header marks are health for the framed session, the engine, and the vault: red when down, gray when idle, cyan when live. They are not window decorations, and they are not the four states. A settled cell and a focused cell differ by border and by color. The border means focus, not inclusion.

Hotkeys for the four states bind on the canvas root only, when that window is focused: Ctrl+Shift+I, Ctrl+Shift+E, Ctrl+Shift+P, and Ctrl+Shift+O. Completing turn N materializes an empty turn N+1. A new conversational turn is not the terminal's new-pane command. Connect, new pane, and close pane still mean SSH panes.

The canvas tabs are conversations inside the notebook. They are not SSH splits. The focused framed session's user is the user whose vault the notebook uses. One tab and one vault follow that focused terminal user. A raw pane leaves the canvas tab unavailable and leaves the terminal tab working. The Java frame keeps the connection strip, collapses it while connected, and on a resize re-asserts the collapsed divider at zero so the strip does not reappear. A later layout note names the divider constant 11. Disconnect restores the last expanded height. Java notebook buttons are beveled, and they are forty percent shorter than the earlier control height, which is the same ratio as sixty percent of that height. A fitted button font floors at 8. Scrollbar arrows at each end are light gray with black arrows. Those pixels are the Java surface. The Rust surface may differ. The window icon is not the server's old metaphor. The motif is an eye crossed with a swoosh, green, blue, and gold on black, including the small sizes from sixteen to thirty-two pixels. The pixels do not block the notebook.

A running cell that crashes becomes interrupted. Streamed text may stay on screen. It is not included until the operator commits it. Failure shows a banner and enables Run again. Status stays running until end, cancel, or error. No vault transaction spans a model call.

A burner executes in memory, paints, and persists metadata and traces with empty payloads. Push of a burner is refused. An export body of a burner is refused. A cloud target is refused unless an allow-cloud-burner policy says otherwise. A burner is not a default cloud send. Dropping the text from the heap is best-effort. A string is not erasable. Logs at the deepest level may show payloads and must never show a burner payload.

Groups are locked direction. They are not the present execute path. When they are built, the operator can promote the focused cell into a group, and that cell becomes the first member. The operator can add a sibling with a different execution target. The operator can remove a member back to the sequential column, or delete it. Members scroll horizontally. A merge cell sits below. The merge algorithm that was chosen is concatenation, with a banner for each model. A model-written merge is not the first merge. It may later be an option on the merge cell. An operator-picked winner was not the choice. Parallel siblings are not in each other's working sets. Layout of a group lives inside the canvas tab and does not follow the terminal splits. Concurrent execution uses the model lane, one in flight per cell, with the interface thread left for paint.

Pipes are the same class of later work. The notebook cut may ship without them. A text push copies a source response into a target prompt and the copy is static. A variable push substitutes `{{cell[k].output}}` at each execute of the target. A chain executes dependencies in topological order. The chain chord named for that work is Ctrl+Shift+F5. The source must be completed. An ephemeral cell cannot push. A cycle fails. A chain stops on a failed cell. The working-set walk ignores siblings unless the cell is a merge or the prompt references another cell's output.

A later canvas shaper is specified and is not the present execute path. It is not a fifth state. The first phase is a keyword filter with no model call on a keystroke. The operator types. The filter splits on whitespace and punctuation and drops the stopwords `a`, `the`, `and`, `of`, and `to`. The remaining tokens are a conjunction of case-insensitive substring matches against the cell's input and output, not against a burner's empty payload. While the pin is on, matches highlight and non-matches dim, and nothing is written until the operator commits. On commit, a non-match becomes excluded. A match keeps input only, output only, or included. A match that was excluded is promoted to included. The four buttons still override after that. The pin stays on until the operator turns it off. A new following cell is filtered the same way. Turning the pin off clears the highlights and leaves the excluded states in place. It does not silently restore. The second phase, only after that filter and only if a shaper model is configured, is one ephemeral system line for the whole conversation. It is not a canvas cell and it is not a terminal turn. If the shaper is missing, the air-gap is on, or the shaper cannot be reached, the phase is skipped and the operator is told the result is keywords only. The default shaper is the same local model already in use. The mini-conversation is modal and ephemeral. Approve appends one system-role shape message to the working set. It is not stuffed into cell payloads. The inspector must show it. Cancel keeps the keyword commit and adds no shape line. The shape is not recomputed until the next approval. Transport is an ordinary execute. Stemming and synonyms belong to that shape phase, not to a third matcher. The filter does not add a wire message, a second memory writer, a fifth state, a search engine, or an embedding store.

A collapsed included cell is still included. Collapse is not the excluded state. The cell still enters the working set that a later filter or shape would see, and a later pipe can still read its output. The inspector lists the chain that would be sent. The Java inspector shows the newest card first. The send order stays oldest first. Soft wrap in that inspector tracks the pane and can use a saved character width whose default is eighty, beside the choice to use it. Those are surface facts of the Java notebook. The Rust surface may differ. The inclusion rules may not.

Crosstalk is operator-explicit and never automatic. A terminal selection, or a last stretch of terminal lines, becomes a new excluded cell only when the operator asks. There is no automatic tag. A cell is written to the terminal only when the operator asks and confirms. A burner is not sent to the terminal. Nothing crosses by default. Terminal chat is not auto-imported into the canvas.

The Java shell's named colors, so the terminal chrome and the prompt do not drift, are these. The focused block cursor is a translucent electric blue. The unfocused cursor is a darker, paler relative of that blue. The menu font is a bright green in the matrix-rain sense, and that green is the menu font only. The terminal foreground stays configurable. The chat prompt is green. The command prompt is blue. The server's color names and the client's interface colors match. The server file may hold the color names. The client file holds the interface colors. A new YAML parser family is not added for this. The Rust chrome may paint a different surface. It does not get a different prompt protocol.

**Truth.** Cells, four inclusion states, a burner pin, one execute in flight, cancel by cell, and a keepalive that does not write memory are the canvas contract. Groups, pipes, the keyword pin, and the shape line are specified in full and are not the present execute path. Crossing to or from the terminal happens only when the operator asks. A burner does not make that crossing.

**Reason.** Four states let a dirty thread sit beside the work that should enter the next prompt, without a tag vocabulary that would become a second router. Showing the set before the run is how the operator trusts the prune. Holding groups and pipes as a full contract, while refusing to pretend they already run, means the next build does not reinvent them and the present build does not fake them.

**Avoidances.** Do not add a fifth state. Do not route by a scope tag. Do not auto-import the terminal. Do not send a burner to the terminal or to a cloud model by default. Do not include uncommitted streamed text. Do not span a vault transaction across a model call. Do not leave a dead graph button on the footer. Do not run a model on the keyword pin's keystrokes. Do not treat collapse as exclusion. Do not require the Rust window to copy Java bevels. Do not implement a group or a pipe on the present execute path.

## The client assembles the working set, and the host does not invent a second one.

Assembly runs on the client. The host receives the built working set. It does not re-decide inclusion.

The walk follows notebook order for cells before the target. Along a graph, the lineage is the target, then its parent, then the root. Siblings are ignored unless the target is a merge or the prompt references another cell's output. Parallel-group siblings are not in each other's working sets. That sibling rule is part of the later group contract. The present sequential walk still skips excluded cells and still sends only what the four states allow.

Then, in order: skip excluded cells, which are the ghosted cells; skip empty ephemeral content; take only the user side of an input-only cell; take only the assistant side of an output-only cell; take the user side and the assistant side of an included cell; resolve variables on the target when pipes exist; append the target prompt. Variable resolution is the later pipe cut. The notebook cut does not resolve variables. The step stays in the rule so the later cut does not invent a different order.

The inspector must show this list, with roles and a byte or token estimate, before Run. The notebook cut has no canvas cap. The estimate is still shown. The terminal's message cap and token cap are a different window. They do not trim the canvas set.

A shape line, when that later phase has been approved, is one system-role message for the entire conversation, appended to the set, shown in the inspector, and not stored as a cell. It is ephemeral. It is not the terminal pack.

The execute that carries the set is the execute body already defined: the set, the cell identifier, the execution target, the knobs, and whether tools are enabled, encoded as TOON inside a length-prefixed envelope. A prune frame may carry a preview of the same kind of set. The host does not persist the preview and does not treat it as hydration. Hydration is the full replace on execute.

The host clears the canvas projection, writes the messages from the set, and calls the one model path. The client paints the response and persists it to the vault unless the cell is a burner.

**Truth.** The working set is built on the client from notebook order, lineage, and the four states, then sent. The host replaces the canvas projection with that set and does not keep a second opinion. The inspector shows the set and an estimate. The notebook cut has no canvas cap and does not resolve pipe variables.

**Reason.** The operator's include and exclude choices are the product. If the host reassembled from a vault it is not allowed to open, or from the terminal pack, those choices would be guesses. A full replace on every execute is simple enough to be deterministic. An estimate without a cap keeps the first notebook honest about cost without hiding turns the operator included.

**Avoidances.** Do not assemble on the host from the vault. Do not let the terminal caps trim the canvas set. Do not skip the inspector. Do not resolve `{{cell[k].output}}` in the notebook cut. Do not put siblings of a parallel group into each other's sets. Do not persist a preview prune. Do not drop the target prompt. Do not send an empty burner payload as if it were content.

## The agent host is one door for a local engine and a remote model, and the tool channel is not the present execute path.

The agentic pillar is the local host inside Casserole. Tools live on the host. A cell calls them. The call is not written into the terminal stream. Tool depth is bounded. The set is an allowlist. Traces of a non-burner call persist in the operator's vault. Until the tool channel is the path a cell actually uses, a cell stays prompt-only. Painting tools into the terminal shell is not the path. The tool lane on the server is named and not allocated until that path is real. The notebook cut runs cell execution on the model lane.

The host wires an agent when that agent implements a published contract: a name, inputs, outputs, a side-effect class, a timeout, and a cancel. A cell names that contract. The vault stores the assembled graph and the traces. The terminal remains the ops view of the box. An agent does not rewrite its own contract. An unbound daemon is not a feature. The host does not invent an agent the operator did not name. Contract assembly, generation of agents, hybrid compute cells, and a cluster of tool hosts are later. They are accounted for so the interface can hold them. They are not the present execute path. A Python execution target is only accounted for. It is not built. Encryption of the vault at rest is not sneaked in early. The graph view waits until its own specification is complete. The graph requirements page was truncated, and a truncated page is not an implementation source. When the graph is built it is ordinary Java graphics, on the client executor, not on a server lane.

The provider interface is one door for a local engine and for a remote model. The present local engine is Ollama. The notebook cut wires that engine and shapes the interface. The remote model is a later target behind that same door. The constitution still calls it a later target. The working specification schedules the first remote implementation after the notebook, and names that implementation Grok. Other vendors may fit the same interface later. They are not built. A builder does not pretend the present execute path already posts to the remote endpoint, and a builder does not design a second door when that endpoint is added. The published URL and the placeholder key in the configuration section are the shape of the door, not a claim that today's cell run uses it.

The router order is locked. If the air-gap is on and the target is a cloud target, the cell fails, a banner is shown, and the stored target is not rewritten. If the local engine is down and the target is local, the cell fails as engine-down, not as an air-gap failure. If the cell is ephemeral and the target is a cloud target and the policy denies it, the cell fails. Otherwise the provider registry runs. The air-gap flag is `aetheris.network.air-gap`. The sample value is false. True forbids cloud targets. In the notebook cut the flag is parsed, and because that cut has no cloud target the flag cannot fire. It is still the law. It is not deleted as dead. The terminal chat keeps the model named in the host configuration until the terminal grows its own picker. Each cell may store an execution target. The notebook's per-cell choice lists the local models the host can see from the engine's tag list, plus the stored target.

`swap`, followed by the model to leave and the model to load, is a terminal command in the notebook cut. It unloads and loads local models for a machine that cannot hold both. It uses the host's existing load and stop. It is a host abstraction, shared, not a second router pasted into the client.

The pool chat is a server contract: one local agent process per SSH user. That contract has no SSH types and no Swing types. What stays off the wire is the client vault, the cloud credential, the burner payload, the tool call as terminal bytes, and any canvas frame. A credential stays out of cell text, unless the cell is a burner, and a burner is not sent to a cloud model by default. Keys live in the environment or under `~/.aetheris/` or `~/.casserole/`. They are not written into this page. The placeholder in the published configuration is not a key.

The host still starts when the local engine is down. A terminal turn then fails visibly, in the error color the terminal already uses. Boot is not the engine.

**Truth.** Tools, traces, and the agent process live on the host. The provider door is one door. The present engine on that door is the local engine. The remote endpoint is the later target, published in shape, not claimed as today's execute. The tool channel, the tool lane, and contract agents are locked and are not the present path. A cell stays prompt-only until the tool channel is the path it actually uses. Credentials, vault bytes, and canvas frames stay off the terminal stream.

**Reason.** A local host the operator can see is the answer to a cloud agent the operator cannot bound. One door means the second model does not fork the router. Failing a cloud target under an air-gap, without rewriting the stored target, means the operator's choice is still there when the air-gap comes off. Keeping the tool channel specified but unused stops a canvas run from pretending it called a tool it cannot yet reach.

**Avoidances.** Do not paint tools into the terminal chat. Do not auto-pipe a tool result into the terminal. Do not allocate the tool lane for the notebook cut. Do not rewrite a stored target when the air-gap refuses it. Do not call engine-down an air-gap error. Do not send a burner to a cloud model by default. Do not put a real key on a page or in a cell. Do not let an agent rewrite its contract or run as an unbound daemon. Do not invent an agent the operator did not name. Do not implement the graph from a truncated page. Do not give the pool contract SSH types or Swing types. Do not open a second model stack in either client.
